title: 強まる海外志向「企業も家計も」　円安下で対外投資加速、10年で倍増
extracted_text:
「人口が増え、住宅不足が見込まれる米国やオーストラリアなどで住宅事業の拡大を図る。国内市場の縮小はある意味、仕方ない」。 住友林業 の光吉敏郎社長はこう話す。同社は2月、42億ドル（6500億円超）を投じて米住宅大手トライ・ポイント・ホームズ（TPH）を買収すると決めた。

買収資金は相対的に金利の低い円建てで調達し、ドルに転換して投資するスキームを組む。為替取引上は円売り・ドル買いの需要が生まれる。

日本企業が成長機会を海外に求める動きが広がっている。海外での工場建設や企業買収などの対外直接投資（実行から回収を引いた純投資額）は2025年におよそ33兆円となった。現行基準で2年連続で過去最高を更新し、10年前からほぼ倍増した。

日本企業は1ドル=70〜80円台の過度な円高を含む「六重苦」に悩まされていた10年代前半から海外投資を拡大してきた。当時は輸出競争力の低下を危惧した製造業の生産拠点の分散が目立った。

ここ数年の円安で海外投資が割高になったにもかかわらず、投資の勢いはむしろ増した。企業の顔ぶれも製造業だけでなく、住宅など内需型産業に広がる。

国内では人口減が加速し、市場の縮小と人手不足という需要・供給の両面でビジネスの継続が難しくなっている。東日本大震災以降の電力不足やサプライチェーン（供給網）の国際分散といった事情も重なり、円安下でも企業の国内回帰の機運は乏しい。

JFEスチールは25年末、インド鉄鋼大手JSWスチールの子会社に約2700億円出資することを決めた。「経済合理性は確認していくが、長い目でみてやるべきことはやらなきゃいけない」。親会社 JFEホールディングス の寺畑雅史取締役は円安下でも海外投資を続ける覚悟を示す。

今後は日本政府がトランプ米政権との通商交渉で合意した5500億ドルの対米投資も実行段階に移る。ドル需要の拡大が持続的な円安を招く構図は一段と強まる。

日本企業が対米投資を増やしても、稼いだドルを円に替えて国内に還流させれば一定の円買い・ドル売りが生じる。だが現状では自動車産業を筆頭に国内メーカーは米国で得た利益を再投資に回し、米工場での能力増強などに充てるケースが多い。

財務省の国際収支統計によると、日本企業が対外投資で得る稼ぎのうち4割は海外にとどまる。こうした企業行動も根強い円安の根底にある。

投資先の海外シフトは家計でも鮮明だ。

三菱UFJアセットマネジメントが世界株に分散投資するインデックス型の投資信託、通称「オルカン」の運用残高が2月に初めて10兆円を突破した。新しい少額投資非課税制度（NISA）を追い風に、残高はわずか1年強で2倍と急増した。同社担当者は「半分以上はつみたて投資で資金が流入している」と話す。

みずほ銀行の唐鎌大輔氏の試算では、25年末の家計の外貨建て資産残高は130兆円と金融資産全体の5.5%を占める。この四半世紀で円建て資産の増加率は6割だったのに対し、外貨建て資産は8倍に膨らんだ。

背景にあるのが「実質的なマイナス金利政策」の継続だ。

日銀の政策金利の引き上げと連動し、限りなくゼロに近かった銀行の預金金利もじわじわと上昇している。2月には三菱UFJ銀行が1年物の円定期預金金利を0.4%と約17年ぶりの高さに引き上げた。

だが消費者物価の前年比上昇率は2%程度での推移が続く。銀行に預金を置いても物価変動を考慮した実質的な利回りはマイナスの状態で、資産が目減りすると気づいた家計は海外に目を向ける。

とりわけ「円依存」への危機感が強いのは現役世代だ。ソニー銀行では、外貨預金口座を持つ顧客の4割が40代以下という。27年開始のこどもNISAでは親や祖父母の円預金の一部が子や孫の口座に移り、海外資産への投資が加速する可能性もある。

円安の招くインフレと実質金利の低下が預金の海外シフトを誘い、さらに円安が定着する――。そんな循環が始まっている。「現状は急性的なキャピタルフライト（海外への資本逃避）とは異なるが、マイルドな逃避が始まっている」。みずほ銀の唐鎌氏はこう警鐘を鳴らす。

translated_text:
The population is increasing, and there is a housing shortage expected in the US, Australia, and other countries, so we are expanding our housing business. The shrinking domestic market is, in a sense, unavoidable." said Toshio Mitsuyoshi, President of Sumitomo Forestry. The company decided in February to acquire US housing giant Try-Point Homes (TPH) by investing $4.2 billion (over ¥650 billion).

The acquisition funds are raised relatively in yen at low interest rates, with a structure to convert to dollars for investment. In foreign exchange transactions, this creates demand for yen selling and dollar buying.

Japanese companies are expanding their search for growth opportunities abroad. Foreign direct investment (net investment after recovery) for factory construction and corporate acquisitions overseas reached approximately ¥33 trillion in 2025. This consecutively broke records under the current standards, nearly doubling from 10 years ago.

Japanese companies had been troubled by the "six difficulties" including excessive yen strength at the 70-80 yen per dollar level since the early 2010s, and they expanded overseas investment from that period. At the time, manufacturing companies were notably dispersing production bases out of fear of declining export competitiveness.

Despite the weaker yen making overseas investment more expensive in recent years, the momentum of investment has rather increased. The mix of companies has also expanded beyond manufacturing to include domestic demand-oriented industries such as housing.

In Japan, population decline is accelerating, and it is becoming difficult to sustain business on both the demand and supply sides due to market shrinkage and labor shortages. Combined with factors such as power shortages since the Great East Japan Earthquake and the international dispersion of supply chains, there is little momentum for companies to return to the domestic market even under the weak yen.

JFE Steel decided at the end of 2025 to invest approximately ¥270 billion in a subsidiary of Indian steel major JSW Steel. "We will examine economic rationality, but from a long-term perspective, we must do what needs to be done." said Masahumi Terahata, Director of parent company JFE Holdings, showing resolve to continue overseas investment even under the weak yen.

Going forward, the $550 billion investment in the US agreed upon by the Japanese government in trade negotiations with the Trump administration will also move to the implementation stage. The structure where increased dollar demand leads to sustained yen weakening will become even stronger.

Even if Japanese companies increase US investment, if they convert earned dollars back to yen and repatriate funds to Japan, a certain amount of yen buying and dollar selling occurs. However, as things stand, domestic manufacturers, led by the automotive industry, often reinvest profits earned in the US into expanding capacity at American factories.

According to the Bank of Japan's balance of payments statistics, about 40% of the earnings from Japanese companies' foreign investment stays overseas. This corporate behavior also underlies the persistent yen weakness.

The shift to overseas investment is also clear among households.

Mitsubishi UFJ Asset Management's index fund that diversifies investment into global stocks, commonly known as "Orukan," saw its assets under management exceed ¥10 trillion for the first time in February. With the new NISA (small investment tax-exempt system) as a tailwind, assets doubled in just over a year. A company representative said, "More than half of the funds are flowing in through periodic investments."

According to calculations by Daisuke Karakama of Mizuho Bank, household foreign currency-denominated assets at the end of 2025 total ¥130 trillion, accounting for 5.5% of total financial assets. Over this quarter century, yen-denominated asset growth was 60%, while foreign currency-denominated assets swelled eightfold.

The backdrop is the continuation of the "effective negative interest rate policy."

Along with the Bank of Japan's policy rate hikes, bank deposit rates, which had been near zero, are gradually rising. In February, Mitsubishi UFJ Bank raised its 1-year yen time deposit rate to 0.4%, the highest in about 17 years.

However, the year-on-year consumer inflation rate remains around 2%. Even if you deposit money in banks, the real return adjusted for price changes is in negative territory, and households realizing their assets are decreasing are looking overseas.

The sense of crisis toward "yen dependence" is particularly strong among the working generation. At Sony Bank, 40% of customers with foreign currency deposit accounts are 40 or younger. With the children NISA starting in 2027, some yen deposits from parents and grandparents may move to children's or grandchildren's accounts, possibly accelerating investment in overseas assets.

Weakening yen bringing inflation and declining real interest rates are prompting deposits to shift overseas, further cementing the weak yen. Such a cycle is beginning. "The current situation is different from acute capital flight, but a mild escape is underway." warns Mr. Karakama of Mizuho Bank.
title_en: Growing Overseas Orientation for Both Companies and Households' - Foreign Investment Accelerates Under Weak Yen, Doubles in 10 Years
